# Module 3. Choosing the parameters {#sec-m3}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**In this chapter.** Set the Explorer's ten controls for a country and record why each one sits where it does. Five carry the heaviest judgment and get the full treatment, beside the control rather than ahead of it: what it is, why it matters, how to set it, what the underlying source shows, a run in the Explorer, and one challenge to answer. The growth assumptions and the interest-rate approach are the assisted layer, their records one CONTEXT click away. Those rationale lines become the assumption section of your export packet, and they preserve the decision record when staff change.

Short on time: do the five self-checks and the ten rationale lines, and skip the explanatory prose. About 25 minutes, and it is the part the capstone rubric marks.
:::

## Why parameter choices need a written record

A year after a projection is built, nobody can say whether 1.2 percent productivity growth was a considered view about the country or a default nobody touched. The analysis is not wrong. It is unusable, because it cannot be defended.

Q-CRAFT Explorer cannot stop you leaving a default in place. What it can do is make the record, so your parameters and your reasons travel with the output.

**One standard covers all ten controls, in two tiers.** A value you changed needs evidence: what you set it to, and what in the country's record supports it. A default you left alone needs a short line saying you reviewed it and kept it, with the reason keeping it was right. The second is a sentence rather than a paragraph. It is also the whole difference between a considered baseline and a run nobody can defend a year later.

Where a parameter's own section below asks for more than that, take the more. Four of the five core calls want a second run beside the line, because their defaults are the ones a result most often turns on.

### Where the retained-default line goes

**The sidebar will not take it, so put it in the analyst's note.** The Explorer opens its **Why this value?** field only on a control you have moved, which leaves an untouched default with nowhere on screen to carry its confirmation. Write those lines into the run label and analyst's note before you export, or into the parameter table you keep beside the run. The annex prints the parameter either way, and your note carries the reason you kept it.

## Seven tabs, and what each one is for

**Seven tabs hold everything the tool shows, and you will move between them and the sidebar constantly.** **Baseline** is the no-climate-change projection. **Analysis** overlays baseline and climate debt paths on one chart. **Climate** shows what warming does to GDP, scenario by scenario. **Data** gives the grid and the two CSV downloads. **Export** assembles the export packet. Your assumptions and rationale sit in its annex. **Methodology** and **About the data** carry the model summary and the exact data releases behind each mode. Reading the charts properly is [Module 4](m4-worked-example.qmd). For now you need only know where to look when a parameter moves.

## What the ten controls do {#sec-m3-core}

Two questions from [Module 1](m1-how-qcraft-thinks.qmd), without looking back:

1. Which of the three numbers do the debt target and the fiscal rule move?
2. Expenditure rigidity of 1.0 means spending is what?

(Answers: the primary balance, through the spending side. Sticky, so the full revenue loss lands on the deficit.)

{{< include figures/_course-map-m3.qmd >}}

Growth takes the demography variant and the growth assumptions, the interest rate takes the approach control, and the primary balance takes the fiscal-policy group.

**Q-CRAFT Explorer has ten user-facing controls, and every one lands on one of the three numbers.** Country selection loads the data everything else runs on, and the demography variant sits beside it. Under **Growth assumptions** sit the productivity and inflation paths, a start and a long-run value each, and the interest-rate approach. Under **Fiscal policy** sit the debt target, the fiscal rule, and expenditure rigidity.

The figure below wires each control to the number it moves. Keep it open while you set the controls.

{{< include figures/_m3-controls.qmd >}}

Five of the ten are the core judgment calls and this module's five sections: country selection, the demography variant, the debt target, the fiscal rule, and expenditure rigidity. Each is a decision no data source can make for you, each taught in full below, each ending in the record the capstone rubric marks. The other five, the growth assumptions and the interest-rate approach, carry published records to read their defaults against. They are the assisted layer.

Every control starts at an engine default. The sidebar keeps the score. Change any control and it gains a CHANGED badge, the engine default printed beside it, and a one-line **Why this value?** field. The export annex prints all ten parameters either way, with your rationale, or with the note that you gave none.

This chapter and the Explorer both put the guidance beside the parameter, the second of the four differences [Module 1](m1-how-qcraft-thinks.qmd) sets out. Each figure here uses the Explorer's own source data and sits beside the parameter it informs. On screen, where a published source has a view, the CONTEXT button beside the parameter opens that source's record for the loaded country, stamped with the data mode, while you set the control. Two buttons, on country selection and the fiscal rule, open a short note instead, because no source publishes a view on them.

### Country selection {#sec-m3-country}

The country dropdown lists every country present in all four of the Explorer's input datasets. That is a test across sources, not a guarantee that every year of every series is present, so a few listed countries still have a hole where the projection needs a figure. Selecting a country loads macroeconomic data from the IMF's World Economic Outlook and population projections from the UN World Population Prospects. Which releases depends on the data mode: Current, the default, runs WEO April 2026 with the UN's 2024 revision, and Verified runs the workbook's own WEO October 2024 with the 2022 revision.

The country you select determines all historical data and every WEO forecast-period projection. No manual data entry: the tool loads real GDP, nominal GDP, revenue, expenditure, debt, interest rates, and demographic projections automatically.

**Choose the country you are analyzing.** Then check the starting point where the tool shows it. The Baseline tab's debt chart opens on the WEO record and forecast, shaded through the horizon, and the Data tab's grid carries the same figures year by year. Investigate before proceeding if the latest debt ratio does not match your understanding.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Country coverage

The dropdown holds 175 countries on each of the two data vintages. Not all 175 produce a projection. Eight or nine, depending on the vintage, are refused outright, because the source lacks something the projection cannot proceed without, most often the primary expenditure figure or the starting debt stock. The Explorer says so on screen rather than drawing a line from a figure that is not there. A few others project from an earlier year than the rest, because the source stopped reporting them before the release ended. For those the tool names the anchor year wherever their results appear. The IMF User Guide [(Tim and Rahman, 2024)](references.qmd#src-user-guide), Section II.B, describes what is loaded for each country.
:::

The whole projection compounds off the starting debt ratio.

{{< include figures/_param-country-context.qmd >}}

Three countries the tool already holds differ in starting debt ratio by more than a factor of three. Hence the first move after selecting a country: check the number the Baseline chart reports.

#### Check the loaded debt ratio against what you already know

1. Predict. Before selecting your country, write down the debt-to-GDP ratio you expect the tool to report, from your own knowledge of its latest position.
2. Observe. Select the country and read the latest figure off the Baseline tab's shaded WEO band, or the same year's row in the Data tab's grid.
3. Explain. If your number and the tool's differ by more than a point or two, work out which is on a different basis before going further. Three causes are common: gross versus net debt, fiscal year versus calendar year, and the WEO vintage lagging the ministry's own outturn. Each is legitimate. Each will be the first question you are asked about your results.

#### Defend it: is this the current debt number?

A reviewer asks: "Is this the current debt number?" Take the worked case (the Uganda run [Module 4](m4-worked-example.qmd) works end to end, the Statement's figures taken as given here). You are running Verified mode, WEO October 2024, and Uganda's FY2024/25 Fiscal Risk Statement reports public debt at 46.9 percent of GDP at June 2023 and projects 49.2 percent at June 2024. What do you say?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## DRAFT FOR TEAL: a defensible answer on vintage
Name the vintage, name the basis, and state which direction the difference runs. "This is WEO October 2024 on a calendar-year basis. The ministry's June 2024 figure is 49.2 percent on a fiscal-year basis. The starting point differs by under a point, and the climate result is a difference between two runs from the same starting point, so it is not sensitive to that gap."

That last claim holds because both runs load the same data and differ only in the climate scenario. It is not a licence to quote a gap computed on one vintage beside a run on another.
:::

#### Record in the packet: country and vintage

The data mode and its releases (every packet file carries the stamp), the starting debt ratio as loaded, and any known difference from your ministry's own figure, with the reason.

### Demography variant {#sec-m3-demography}

The UN publishes population projections in three variants, Medium, High and Low, reflecting different fertility assumptions. This parameter selects which variant Q-CRAFT uses for population and labor force projections through 2100.

Working-age population growth, ages 15 to 64, drives employment growth in Q-CRAFT's growth identity after the WEO forecast horizon. Higher population growth means a larger labor force, higher potential GDP, and, all else equal, more favourable debt dynamics. Countries facing demographic decline see slower growth and harder fiscal trajectories. Total population growth matters separately. Primary spending grows with it (see [Module 1](m1-how-qcraft-thinks.qmd) for the expenditure growth formula).

**Medium is the default and the standard assumption for most policy analysis:**

- Use **Medium** unless you have a specific reason to explore demographic scenarios.
- Use **High** and **Low** where fertility trends are uncertain or where you expect demographic policy to change.
- For countries in rapid demographic transition, with a declining working-age population, compare Medium against Low to see how sensitive the fiscal path is to the demographic outcome.

Detailed methodology: [the IMF User Guide, pp. 10-12](references.qmd#src-user-guide) and Section IV.A on demography and employment.

The three variants are the UN's own account of how uncertain its projection is, and how far apart they run depends on where the country is in its demographic transition.

{{< include figures/_param-demography-variants.qmd >}}

Where the working-age population is still climbing the three variants barely separate. Where it has turned down, the choice between Low and High is the difference between a workforce at a quarter of today's and one at three quarters.

#### Does the variant move Ethiopia or Thailand more?

1. Predict. Ethiopia has one of the world's youngest populations. Thailand's working-age population has already started to fall. Before touching the control, will switching from Medium to High move Ethiopia's 2099 debt ratio a lot, a little, or barely at all? Write down a direction and a rough size in percentage points, then a second prediction for Thailand.
2. Observe. Run Ethiopia, switch between Medium and High, and watch the Baseline tab's debt trajectory. Then run Thailand and do the same. Compare the size of the two moves.
3. Explain. In countries with young, growing populations the variants barely separate over the projection, because the working-age share is already rising in every variant. In countries facing demographic decline the gap widens sharply: slower working-age growth means lower GDP growth and rising expenditure-to-GDP ratios at the same time. Both effects run through $g$: the expenditure channel through total population, the growth channel through working-age population, and the two populations move differently, which is why the net effect is not obvious in advance.

#### Defend it: a colleague wants the Low variant

A colleague argues for the Low variant, because your country's fertility rate has been falling faster than the UN projected. Do you switch?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## DRAFT FOR TEAL: a defensible answer on the demography variant
Probably not for the headline run. Certainly worth a sensitivity run. Medium is the reference variant, and using anything else as your headline leaves you defending a demographic forecast inside a fiscal risk document. The colleague's point is testable in two minutes: run Low, record the difference in the 2099 debt ratio, and put the number in the packet as a sensitivity. A small difference retires the objection with evidence. A large one is worth a paragraph.
:::

#### Record in the packet: the demography variant

The variant chosen, why in one line (Medium is the default, so the line says you reviewed it and kept it), and the 2099 debt ratio under at least one alternative variant as a sensitivity.

### Debt target (% of GDP) {#sec-m3-target}

The debt target is the debt-to-GDP ratio the fiscal rule steers toward over time. The range runs from 0 to 200 percent of GDP.

The target does nothing until the fiscal rule is enabled, and then it determines how hard spending has to adjust. A target below current debt calls for consolidation, which cuts primary expenditure. A higher target calls for less adjustment.

**Start from the country's actual fiscal framework.** Many countries legislate debt targets in their fiscal rules. Use them where they exist. Uganda's FY2024/25 Fiscal Risk Statement reads its climate results against a 50 percent of GDP fiscal rule ceiling and reports public debt passing it in the High, Hot and Vulnerable scenarios (Vulnerable is the Statement's label for the Explorer's Hot + Unadapted, and the naming note in [Module 1](m1-how-qcraft-thinks.qmd) has the mapping). Where no formal target exists, the debt-stabilizing primary balance is a standard DSA benchmark (see [the IMF User Guide, Section IV.A](references.qmd#src-user-guide), and Step 1 of [Module 2](m2-debt-equation.qmd)).

Common practice offers three rough starting points, none of them authoritative IMF guidance:

- Low-income countries (LICs): 40 to 50 percent of GDP is a common range in practice, broadly consistent with IMF-World Bank Debt Sustainability Framework thresholds.
- Emerging markets (EMs): 50 to 70 percent of GDP, depending on market access, institutional quality, and fiscal track record.
- Advanced economies (AEs): can sustain higher ratios, 60 to 100 percent and above, though the appropriate target depends on growth prospects and market confidence.

Detailed methodology: [the IMF User Guide, pp. 15-18](references.qmd#src-user-guide) on fiscal rule assumptions and the baseline scenario.

The target has no source figure: a policy choice rather than a published series. The nearest evidence is the country's own record, the debt-ratio figure at the top of this module, read against whatever anchor your fiscal framework already sets.

#### What moving the target from 40 to 80 does to spending

1. Predict. With the fiscal rule enabled, you are about to move the debt target from 40 percent to 80 percent. Write down what happens to primary expenditure in the early years and to the 2099 debt ratio.
2. Observe. Set the target to 40, read the primary expenditure path and the debt path in the Baseline tab. Set it to 80 and read them again.
3. Explain. A lower target forces faster consolidation, so expenditure is cut harder to bring debt down. A higher target leaves more spending room. The adjustment is gradual rather than immediate, because it works through the fiscal gap over several years. If you predicted an instant jump in expenditure, correct that: the rule is a feedback loop keyed to last year's debt position, not a switch.

#### Defend it: a reviewer asks for a lower target "to be prudent"

You are asked to run the projection against a 40 percent target rather than the 50 percent ceiling your fiscal risk documentation already uses. What do you do, and what do you say?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## DRAFT FOR TEAL: a defensible answer on the debt target
Run both, and say what the target does in the model. In Q-CRAFT the debt target is not a judgment about what is sustainable. It is the anchor the simulated fiscal rule steers toward, so changing it changes the assumed policy reaction rather than the country's risk. Give both numbers: "At the 50 percent anchor, the Hot scenario breaches the ceiling by X. At a 40 percent anchor, staying inside it requires Y percent of GDP a year of additional primary balance." That answers the request without smuggling a policy preference into a risk assessment.
:::

#### Record in the packet: the debt target

The target used, its source (legislated rule, Charter for Fiscal Responsibility, DSF threshold, analyst judgment), and the alternative target you tested.

### Fiscal rule (Yes / No) {#sec-m3-rule}

The fiscal rule, when enabled, adjusts primary expenditure to steer debt toward the target ratio. When disabled, spending follows baseline trends whatever the debt level does.

Without a fiscal rule, debt dynamics are purely mechanical. They follow the interest-growth differential and whatever primary balance falls out of revenue and expenditure trends. With the rule on, the model simulates active fiscal policy: the government cuts spending as debt rises or spends more as fiscal space opens.

**Run it both ways, rule off first:**

- Start with the fiscal rule off to see the "no policy change" baseline: is debt stable, rising, or falling under current trends?
- Turn the fiscal rule on to answer a different question: how much consolidation would reaching the debt target take?

Most countries have some form of fiscal anchor in practice, though enforcement varies. The IMF User Guide notes Q-CRAFT's fiscal rule is an approximation: it does not model the GDP effects of fiscal consolidation [(User Guide, p. 17, footnote 11)](references.qmd#src-user-guide).

The adjustment lands on the level of primary expenditure rather than its growth rate. It is applied after the multiplicative growth factors and depends on the prior year's state, so Q-CRAFT computes it recursively, year by year.

#### How much the rule changes your country's 2099 ratio

1. Predict. Run your country with the rule off first. Will turning the rule on change the 2099 debt ratio a lot or a little? Reason from where the off-rule path ends relative to the target.
2. Observe. Run the same country with the fiscal rule on and off. Watch both the debt path and the primary expenditure path.
3. Explain. With the rule off and unfavourable dynamics, the interest rate exceeding growth, debt-to-GDP can rise without bound. Turn the rule on and debt converges toward your target, the primary expenditure chart showing the spending cuts required. The gap between the two runs is the fiscal effort your target implies. If the off-rule path already sits near the target, turning the rule on does almost nothing. Report that.

#### Defend it: which run belongs in a Fiscal Risk Statement?

Rule on or rule off?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## DRAFT FOR TEAL: a defensible answer on rule on or off
Both belong, because they answer different questions. Rule **off** is the risk statement: where we end up if policy does not respond, shown as the sensitivity beside the rule-on headline run (Step 1 of [Module 4](m4-worked-example.qmd) makes rule on the headline, and when a rule-off baseline hits the zero debt floor the comparison breaks, see [the debt floor rule](m5-boundaries.qmd#sec-m5-floor)). Rule **on** is the policy statement: the effort required to hold the anchor. Publishing only the rule-on run understates the risk, because it assumes the response you are trying to justify. Publishing only the rule-off run invites the objection that no government would sit still for seventy years. Report the pair and say which is which.
:::

#### Record in the packet: the fiscal rule

Rule on or off for the headline run, and the reason, which is a reviewed-and-kept line where the run keeps the engine's setting, the paired run, and one sentence on which question each answers.

### Expenditure rigidity (0.0 - 1.0) {#sec-m3-rigidity}

Expenditure rigidity measures how far government spending resists downward adjustment when climate shocks reduce GDP. It affects climate scenarios only, never the baseline.

**Rigidity decides how much of the climate cost becomes debt.** When climate change reduces GDP, revenue falls with it, because revenue tracks nominal GDP. What happens to spending settles the rest.

- **1.0 (fully rigid, worst case):** spending stays at its baseline level in local currency even as GDP falls, so the entire climate impact passes through to the primary balance and the debt ratio. This is a government that cannot or will not cut spending: a large civil service wage bill, entitlement programmes, or political constraints.
- **0.0 (fully flexible):** spending falls in proportion with GDP, holding the expenditure-to-GDP ratio at its baseline level. The debt impact of climate change is smaller, because the government absorbs the shock by reducing real spending per person.
- **Values between 0 and 1** represent partial adjustment. Most countries sit in between: some categories are rigid (wages, pensions, debt service) while others can adjust (capital investment, discretionary programmes).

Start from the composition of the budget:

- Countries with large public sector wage bills, universal social programmes, or rigid entitlement commitments: lean toward 0.7 to 1.0.
- Countries with more fiscal flexibility, smaller governments, or well-established expenditure review processes: 0.3 to 0.6.

The default of 1.0 is conservative by construction. It shows the worst case, where all climate damage becomes additional borrowing. The defensible way to use it is to run 1.0 as the headline and a lower value as the sensitivity, saying in one line why: a fiscal risk statement is the document where conservatism belongs.

Detailed methodology: [the IMF User Guide, pp. 20 and 35-36](references.qmd#src-user-guide) on the expenditure rigidity parameter and fiscal effects of climate change.

Rigidity is a claim about how spending has behaved, and the WEO record carries evidence on it.

{{< include figures/_param-rigidity-record.qmd >}}

Read the revenue and expenditure lines against each other rather than separately. Revenue holds a roughly constant share of GDP by construction in the projection but moves in the historical record, and the question is what expenditure did when it moved. A budget whose expenditure ratio climbs while revenue falls has behaved as though rigidity is high. That is evidence you can put in the packet, stronger than a view about political will.

::: {.callout-warning .authoring-note}

#### Which rigidity value widens the fan, and by how much

1. Predict. On the Analysis tab you are about to compare the climate fan at rigidity 1.0 against 0.0. Write down which produces the wider fan, and by roughly what factor.
2. Observe. Set rigidity to 1.0 and read the 2099 gap between the baseline and Hot + Unadapted. Set it to 0.0 and read the same gap.
3. Explain. Then put rigidity back to the value your headline run uses, so the run you export is the one you meant. At 1.0 the fan spreads wide, because the whole climate revenue loss accumulates as debt, so the Paris-Aligned to Hot + Unadapted distance is large. At 0.0 the scenarios compress toward the baseline, because the government absorbs the shock through spending. The distance between the two fans is your country's fiscal exposure to expenditure rigidity, usually the largest single lever in the tool. If you predicted rigidity matters less than the choice of climate scenario, check that prediction. For most countries it is wrong.

{{< include figures/_screenshot-m3-rigidity-compare.qmd >}}

#### Defend it: one colleague calls 1.0 alarmist, another calls anything lower wishful

A colleague says 1.0 is alarmist: "no government holds spending flat in local currency for seventy years while the economy shrinks." Another says anything below 1.0 assumes a fiscal discipline your country has not demonstrated. What do you do?

::: {.callout-important collapse="true"}
## DRAFT FOR TEAL: defending a rigidity choice

Both colleagues are making empirical claims. Settle them with evidence rather than adjectives.

The evidence to reach for is the composition of the budget, not a view about political will. The share of primary expenditure in wages, pensions, statutory transfers and other commitments requiring legislation to change is close to a floor on rigidity. In most low-income countries it is high, and the flexible remainder is dominated by domestically financed development spending, the spending a government cuts first.

**The defensible position** is to run 1.0 as the headline and a lower value as the sensitivity, saying why in one line: the default is conservative by design, and a fiscal risk statement is the document where conservatism belongs. The sensitivity run gives the second colleague their number: at rigidity 0.6, the 2099 gap narrows from X to Y percentage points.

What not to do is pick a middle value because it feels balanced. An unexplained 0.5 is weaker than 1.0 with a stated rationale, because 1.0 at least has the tool's own conservative-default argument attached. A middle number with no reasoning is the assumption that gets quietly reused for five years by people who never knew it was a guess.

The sentence for the packet: "Rigidity set at 1.0, the tool default, because roughly N percent of primary expenditure is wages, pensions and statutory commitments. The sensitivity run at 0.6 changes the 2099 climate-baseline debt gap from X to Y percentage points."
:::

#### Record in the packet: expenditure rigidity

The rigidity used (1.0 is the default, and keeping it is a decision that still earns its line), the budget-composition evidence behind it, and the sensitivity run and its effect on the headline gap. Run 1.0 against 0.0 to see the mechanism at its extremes, and report a plausible second value such as 0.6 as the sensitivity. This is the entry the capstone rubric weights most heavily.

## The assisted layer: growth assumptions and the interest-rate approach

The five remaining controls are assumptions about the future, and the Explorer puts the published record beside each one. Productivity growth and inflation each take a start and a long-run value. The interest-rate approach picks which of the three rate rules from [Module 1](m1-how-qcraft-thinks.qmd) runs, the constant nominal rate by default. All five start at engine defaults, so an untouched run is the defaults' run and the annex will say so. Saying so is not the same as defending it, which is what the retained-default line is for.

Two of those defaults are worth seeing against the record they are meant to continue. Productivity growth slides from 5.0 percent to 1.2 percent, and inflation from 5.0 percent to 3.5 percent, for every country in the tool.

{{< include figures/_param-productivity.qmd >}}

{{< include figures/_param-inflation.qmd >}}

Neither figure tells you the default is wrong. The productivity figure shows what a single global productivity path is averaging over, and the inflation figure does the same for a single global inflation path. Where your country's record sits well above or well below either default, write the sentence you would want on the record: *the run keeps the engine's global default of 1.2 percent long-run productivity growth, and this country's own record runs above it.* Name the assumption, name the default, and name which side your country sits on.

In the Explorer, that comparison is one click. The CONTEXT button beside each growth assumption opens the same record for the loaded country, places your setting against it, and offers a computed sentence you can add to the rationale. The interest-rate approach gets the same treatment, and [Module 2](m2-debt-equation.qmd)'s interest-rules comparison is the reason to look: for Kenya, the three approaches disagree by thirty-one points of GDP by 2099.

**A changed growth assumption earns the same line in the annex as the five core calls.** A moved one is a claim about your country's future, and the record behind the CONTEXT button is where its defence starts. A retained one earns the shorter line: the default was read against that record and kept, and here is why keeping it was right.

## What you can now do

- You can set the five core judgment calls for a country and give a reason for each that cites evidence rather than preference, and you know where the assisted layer's records live.
- You can predict each parameter's direction of effect, and its rough magnitude, before moving it, which tells you when the tool is behaving oddly.
- You can defend an expenditure rigidity choice against a colleague who prefers a different one.
- You have ten rationale lines, one per control: five from the core calls and five from the assisted layer. Together they are the assumption-rationale section of your export packet.

Three errors recur on this material: inverting the rigidity scale (see [Module 0](m0-start-here.qmd), question 2), moving the debt target while the fiscal rule is off and wondering why nothing happened, and choosing a middle value to avoid an argument.

On your desk this week: find one number in a projection your department published and ask who chose it and why. If the answer takes more than a minute to find, you have made the case for the export packet.
